summaries.example: Imagine two apples. Each apple has its own particular redness. The redness of one apple is not the very same thing as the redness of the other, but the two rednesses can look exactly alike. A trope theorist says these are two different redness-tropes that resemble each other.
summaries.summary: Trope theory is a philosophical idea about what the world is made of. It says that particular features—such as the exact color of this leaf or the exact weight of this stone—are real. These features are called tropes. Two leaves may both be green, but each has its own green trope. Their tropes are different things that resemble each other. This gives trope theory a middle position between two older ideas. One idea says that general features, called universals, are real and can be present in many objects. Another says that only individual objects exist and that similarities do not require special features. Trope theorists try to explain both how things are alike and how they remain different. Some say objects are bundles of tropes. Others think objects also need a separate underlying bearer. Philosophers further debate whether tropes are simple, how they are individuated, and whether they help explain perception, causes, language, science, or value.
key_ideas: A trope is one thing’s own particular feature, not a general feature shared by all things.
Different objects can have tropes that exactly resemble one another.
Some philosophers think tropes are the basic pieces from which objects are built.
Philosophers disagree about whether tropes are more like properties, objects, or something between them.
They also disagree about what makes two similar tropes different and how tropes join together into objects.
summaries.why_it_matters: Trope theory offers a way to talk about real features without saying that one general feature must be literally present in many different objects. It may help explain why a hot pan burns a hand: this pan’s particular heat seems more directly involved than heat in general. But the source also emphasizes that these arguments are debated, because other theories can explain many of the same facts.

important_terms.definition: A particular feature belonging to one thing, such as the exact redness, weight, or shape of one apple.
A feature that can be shared by many things, such as redness in general.
The view that ordinary things are made from a group, or bundle, of tropes.
A relation in which two particular features are alike in the relevant way.

questions_to_think_about: If two socks have exactly the same color, do they have one color or two particular color-features?
Could a feature exist without belonging to an object?
What makes two perfectly similar features different?
When you notice an apple’s redness, are you noticing the apple, its redness, or both?

summaries.example: Consider two copper wires that have exactly the same electrical resistance. A trope theorist can say that each wire contains its own resistance-trope. The tropes are numerically distinct—there are two of them—but exactly resemble one another. A universal realist would instead appeal to one repeatable resistance universal, while a classical nominalist may try to explain the similarity without adding property-like entities.
summaries.summary: Trope theory holds that reality is wholly or partly composed of particularized properties: the exact shape, mass, color, or texture of an individual. Two objects do not literally share one numerically identical property; rather, each contains a distinct trope, and the tropes may exactly resemble one another. This position is often intended to occupy a middle ground. Unlike classical nominalism, it takes property-like features seriously enough to explain similarity and difference. Unlike universal realism, it does not require repeatable universals that are present in many instances. The entry stresses that there is no single complete trope theory. Some versions make tropes the only fundamental category, while others add substances, powers, relations, or other entities. Important disputes concern whether a trope is property-like or object-like, whether it is simple, and what individuates it. Further problems arise when tropes are used to construct universals through resemblance classes or to construct concrete objects through bundles. The theory has proposed applications in causation, persistence, mental causation, perception, semantics, physics, and value theory, but the source presents these as contested arguments rather than settled results.
key_ideas: Trope theory has a thin core—tropes exist—but competing versions disagree about almost everything beyond that core.
Tropes are often presented as a middle position between universal realism and classical nominalism: they preserve property-like structure while denying repeatable universals.
Some theories treat tropes primarily as dependent ways objects are; others treat them as object-like building blocks, and some recent discussions use the modifier/module distinction instead.
Most trope theorists regard tropes as ontologically simple in the sense that they are not made from entities of other categories, although they may still have trope-parts or qualitative complexity.
Individuation may be explained by different locations in spacetime, or it may be taken as primitive. Each option faces arguments involving possibilities such as swapping or piling similar tropes.
If objects are bundles, compresence must explain their unity. Treating compresence as an external relation can generate Bradley’s regress, so theorists propose several competing solutions.
summaries.why_it_matters: Tropes show how a metaphysical theory can begin with familiar observations—particular colors, weights, causal effects, and perceptual features—and develop a detailed account of what is fundamental. The theory also makes clear that a seemingly simple question, such as what it means for two objects to be alike, can lead to difficult issues about identity, dependence, explanation, and regress. Comparing trope theory with universals, nominalism, and states-of-affairs theories helps clarify what different ontologies explain well and what costs they incur.

important_terms.definition: A particularized property-instance, such as the exact mass or color located in one object at one time.
A repeatable entity that can be wholly present in more than one particular, such as redness in general.
An account treating objects as organized bundles of mutually related tropes rather than as objects with a separate substrate.
The metaphysical question of what makes two tropes distinct, even when they exactly resemble one another.
The relation by which tropes are joined into a concrete particular or object.
A regress in which each proposed relation joining entities requires another relation to join it, threatening the original explanation.
The claim that some fact or entity has no deeper metaphysical analysis or explanation within the theory.
The problem of explaining how distinct objects can have properties in common.

questions_to_think_about: Does a theory gain explanatory power by replacing universals with resemblance classes of tropes, or does it merely rename the problem?
Should exact resemblance itself be treated as an additional relation, or does it follow from the natures of the tropes?
Would spatiotemporal location adequately individuate tropes if some reality were non-spatiotemporal?
Can a bundle of tropes form one object without a separate substrate or an unexplained unifying relation?
Do perceptual experience and causation favor tropes over states of affairs, or are those data compatible with rival theories?

summaries.example: Suppose two students bring identical-looking blue notebooks. One account says both notebooks share one universal, blueness. Another says there are just two notebooks and no extra property is needed. Trope theory says each notebook has its own blue trope. The two tropes are different, but they exactly resemble each other. This explains both their similarity and the fact that the notebooks are not one object.
summaries.summary: Trope theory is the view that reality includes tropes: particular features belonging to particular things. The exact weight of one backpack and the exact color of one leaf would be tropes. If another backpack has the same weight, it has a different weight-trope that exactly resembles the first. Trope theory therefore tries to explain two facts at once: objects can be similar, yet their features can remain particular and non-identical. This contrasts with universal realism, which appeals to one repeatable property, and with classical nominalism, which does not accept properties as separate entities. The source explains that “trope theory” covers several different positions. Some philosophers make tropes the basic ingredients of everything. Many say ordinary objects are bundles of tropes, while others add a substrate—an underlying bearer—in which tropes are present. Further debates ask whether tropes are more like properties or objects, whether they are simple, and how they are individuated. The theory also proposes that resemblance classes can play the role of universals. Yet connecting tropes into objects raises a difficult regress problem involving compresence. Applications to causation, perception, language, science, mind, and value remain philosophical proposals, not universally accepted conclusions.
key_ideas: Trope theory says that individual features are real, but it does not usually say that one identical feature is present in many objects.
It aims to explain similarity and difference together: resembling tropes are alike in quality but remain numerically separate.
Some versions say tropes are the only basic ingredients of reality; others combine them with substances, powers, or relations.
A major disagreement is whether tropes are property-like ways an object is or object-like pieces that can help build everything else.
The theory must explain how tropes become a whole object and what makes one trope different from another.
Arguments from perception and causation may support trope theory, but similar arguments may also support states of affairs or events.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because it examines the hidden structure behind ordinary descriptions such as “this leaf is green” or “this stove is hot.” Trope theory asks whether the important feature is a general property, a particular instance, a state of affairs, or something else. Studying the competing answers helps us see why metaphysics is not only about naming things: it is about explaining similarity, difference, identity, change, and the connections among parts of reality.

important_terms.definition: A particular instance of a feature belonging to one object, such as the exact blueness of one notebook.
A general property that can occur in many different objects at once.
The view that similarities can be explained by classes of tropes that resemble one another.
A theory saying that an ordinary object is made from a connected group of tropes.
What explains why two tropes are different, even if they are exactly alike in quality.
A proposed relation that holds different tropes together as parts of one object.
A chain of explanations in which each new explanation needs another explanation of the same kind.
The view that something is basic and does not have a further metaphysical explanation.

questions_to_think_about: Which explanation of the blue notebooks seems strongest: a shared universal, two objects with no extra properties, or two resembling tropes?
If two tropes are exactly alike, what could make them different?
Could a group of features make one object without needing a separate thing to hold them together?
Does seeing a leaf change color show that a particular color-feature disappeared?
Why might a philosopher prefer a simpler theory with fewer basic kinds of things?
